items.q: A 32-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed vehicle collision. Imaging demonstrates an anteroposterior compression type III (APC III) pelvic ring disruption with severe hemodynamic instability. Which of the following is the most common source of arterial bleeding in such severe pelvic fractures?
items.e: Although 80–90% of pelvic fracture hemorrhage is venous or from cancellous bone, arterial bleeding occurs in 10–15% of cases. The superior gluteal artery (at the greater sciatic notch) is the most commonly injured arterial vessel, followed by the internal pudendal and obturator arteries.
items.note: Accurate, clear single-best answer question on a high-yield pelvic trauma topic supported by Campbell's/Rockwood.

items.q: An outlet radiograph of the pelvis is obtained by angling the X-ray beam cephalad by 40 to 45 degrees. Which of the following structural parameters is best evaluated on this projection?
items.e: The outlet view (angled 40–45 degrees cephalad) demonstrates vertical displacement of the hemipelvis and sacral foramina. The inlet view (angled 25–45 degrees caudally) demonstrates anteroposterior displacement and pelvic rotation.
items.note: Standard radiograph projection question directly aligned with standard orthopaedic trauma teaching.

items.q: A 45-year-old man sustains a sacral fracture that extends medial to the sacral foramina into the central canal (Denis Zone III). Which of the following clinical features is most characteristically associated with fractures in this specific zone?
items.e: Denis Zone III sacral fractures involve the central canal medial to the foramina and carry the highest rate of neurological injury (~57%), characteristically presenting with bowel, bladder, and sexual dysfunction. Zone I involves the sacral ala (L5 root) and Zone II involves the foramina (sciatica).
items.note: Factually flawless, testing classic sacral fracture classification and clinical correlations.

items.q: A 28-year-old male presents following a crush injury to the pelvis. On physical examination, there is blood present at the external urethral meatus, a perineal hematoma, and a high-riding prostate on digital rectal examination. Which of the following is the correct initial diagnostic step?
o: Blind insertion of a 16-Fr Foley catheter
Placement of a suprapubic catheter without imaging
items.e: Blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate, and perineal hematoma indicate a posterior urethral injury (common in APC and straddle injuries). A retrograde urethrogram must be performed before any catheterisation attempt to evaluate urethral integrity and avoid converting a partial tear to a complete disruption.
items.note: Essential ATLS and orthopaedic emergency principles question, fully supported by reference notes.

items.q: On standard Judet 45-degree oblique radiographic views of the acetabulum, which column and wall are primarily profiled on the obturator oblique view?
items.e: The obturator oblique Judet view profiles the anterior column and posterior wall of the acetabulum, along with the obturator foramen. The iliac oblique view profiles the posterior column and anterior wall.
items.note: Core radiographic anatomy concept in acetabular trauma assessment.

items.q: A 38-year-old male sustains a severe acetabular injury. Radiographs show a 'spur sign' on the obturator oblique view, and CT confirms that no articular fragment remains connected to the intact axial skeleton of the ilium. According to Letournel, this injury pattern is:
items.e: A both-column fracture is an associated acetabular fracture pattern where no articular segment remains attached to the intact axial ilium. The pathognomonic 'spur sign' on the obturator oblique view represents the intact posterior portion of the iliac bone projecting above the displaced articular surface.
items.note: Definitive classification diagnostic feature question, perfectly clear single answer.

items.q: During an anterior intrapelvic (modified Stoppa) approach for acetabular fracture fixation, which vessel located behind the superior pubic ramus approximately 4 to 6 cm from the pubic symphysis is at high risk of injury?
items.e: The corona mortis is an anastomotic vessel between the external iliac/inferior epigastric and obturator vessels situated behind the superior pubic ramus, about 4–6 cm from the symphysis. It is at significant risk during Stoppa and ilioinguinal approaches.
items.note: High-yield surgical anatomy concept frequently tested in superspeciality entrance exams.

items.q: A 26-year-old male suffers a posterior hip dislocation with a femoral head fracture located cephalad to (above) the fovea capitis in the weight-bearing dome. According to the Pipkin classification, this injury is classified as:
items.e: Pipkin Type II fractures are femoral head fractures located cephalad to (above) the fovea capitis, involving the main weight-bearing portion of the femoral head. Type I fractures are caudal to the fovea, Type III includes a femoral neck fracture, and Type IV has an associated acetabular fracture.
items.note: Standard Pipkin classification question with clear distinction between Type I and Type II.

items.q: A 28-year-old male sustains a high-energy femoral neck fracture. Radiographs show a fracture line inclined at 60° relative to the horizontal (Pauwels Grade III). Which statement regarding this fracture pattern is correct?
o: It is an incomplete valgus-impacted fracture with low risk of non-union
It represents a vertical shear pattern with the highest risk of non-union and fixation failure
It is an extracapsular fracture that reliably achieves spontaneous union
It is best managed non-operatively with non-weight-bearing crutch walking
items.e: Pauwels Grade III fractures have a fracture angle greater than 50 degrees from the horizontal plane. This orientation creates high vertical shear forces, resulting in the highest rates of non-union and fixation failure among Pauwels types.
items.note: Accurate, standard Pauwels classification question directly aligned with exam requirements.

items.q: A 78-year-old woman presents with a reverse obliquity intertrochanteric femoral fracture (AO/OTA 31A3). Why is a dynamic sliding hip screw (DHS) contraindicated in this fracture pattern?
o: The side plate cannot accommodate the proximal femoral anatomy
The fracture fragment slides medially along the axis of the lag screw
It completely severs the medial femoral circumflex artery
The tension band effect causes uncontrollable varus collapse
items.e: In reverse obliquity intertrochanteric fractures, the dynamic sliding hip screw (DHS) is contraindicated because the shaft fragment slides medially along the lag screw axis. Unstable patterns such as reverse obliquity require a cephalomedullary nail.
items.note: Classic biomechanical question frequently tested in orthopaedic superspeciality exams.

items.q: In a subtrochanteric fracture of the femur, which group of muscles acts on the proximal fracture fragment to deform it into flexion, abduction, and external rotation?
o: Adductor longus, adductor magnus, and gracilis
Iliopsoas, gluteus medius/minimus, and short external rotators
Vastus lateralis, rectus femoris, and sartorius
items.e: The proximal fragment in a subtrochanteric fracture is deformed into flexion by the iliopsoas, abduction by the gluteus medius and minimus, and external rotation by the short external rotators. The distal shaft is pulled into adduction by the adductors.
items.note: High-yield anatomy question standard for subtrochanteric fracture deforming forces.

items.q: During fixation of an undisplaced femoral neck fracture using parallel cannulated screws, screw insertion below the level of the lesser trochanter should be avoided primarily to prevent:
o: Disruption of the lateral epiphyseal retinacular vessels
Creating a stress riser that increases the risk of a subtrochanteric fracture
Damage to the artery of the ligamentum teres
items.e: Placing a cannulated screw entry point below the level of the lesser trochanter creates a stress riser in the subtrochanteric cortical bone. This significantly increases the risk of an iatrogenic subtrochanteric femoral fracture.
items.note: Well-established surgical principle and entry-point trap tested in entrance exams.

items.q: A patient with a diaphyseal femoral fracture develops respiratory insufficiency, neurological dysfunction, and a petechial rash over the axilla and conjunctiva 48 hours after trauma. According to the Gurd and Wilson criteria, which of these features is classified as a major criterion for fat embolism syndrome?
items.e: Under the Gurd and Wilson criteria for fat embolism syndrome, the major criteria comprise respiratory insufficiency, cerebral signs, and a petechial rash (typically over the axilla, chest, or conjunctiva).
items.note: Factually precise question on standard clinical criteria for Fat Embolism Syndrome.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman on long-term bisphosphonates presents with prodromal thigh pain and an incomplete atypical subtrochanteric femoral fracture showing lateral cortical beaking. What is the initial medical management step for this patient?
o: Discontinue the bisphosphonate, administer calcium/vitamin D, and consider teriparatide
Increase the bisphosphonate dosage to enhance cortical bone density
Start oral corticosteroids while maintaining the bisphosphonate schedule
Apply a long leg cast without modifying her systemic osteoporosis medications
items.e: Management of bisphosphonate-associated atypical femoral fractures includes stopping the bisphosphonate, ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and considering teriparatide. Prophylactic intramedullary nailing is indicated for incomplete fractures accompanied by pain or a visible fracture line.
items.note: Accurate guideline-based medical management question for AFF.

items.q: A 35-year-old male sustains a traumatic intra-articular coronal fracture of the lateral femoral condyle (Hoffa fracture / AO/OTA 33B3). What is the recommended surgical construct for fixation?
o: Anteroposterior lag screws placed perpendicular to the fracture line
Transverse K-wires with a figure-of-eight tension band
items.e: A Hoffa fracture is a coronal plane intra-articular fracture of a femoral condyle (most commonly the lateral condyle). Standard operative fixation involves placing anteroposterior lag screws perpendicular to the fracture plane.
items.note: Directly supported by Campbell's and standard trauma guidelines.

items.q: A 34-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a high-speed motor vehicle collision. Radiographs reveal a Schatzker IV medial tibial plateau fracture-dislocation. Vascular assessment of the injured extremity demonstrates an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) of 0.78. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Immediate open reduction and dual-plate fixation
items.e: An ankle-brachial index (ABI) of less than 0.9 in high-energy tibial plateau fractures (particularly Schatzker IV/VI and bicondylar injuries) indicates potential popliteal artery injury and mandates an arterial imaging study.
items.note: Accurate, standard concept direct from reference notes and Campbell's guidelines.

items.q: According to the classic four-step Rüedi-Allgöwer principles for open reduction and internal fixation of comminuted tibial pilon (plafond) fractures, which step should be performed FIRST in the surgical sequence?
o: Reconstruction of the joint articular surface
Bone grafting of the metaphyseal defect
Buttressing of the medial tibial cortex
items.e: The classic Rüedi-Allgöwer principles outline a four-step sequence for pilon fracture reconstruction: (1) restore fibular length, (2) reconstruct the articular surface, (3) bone graft the metaphyseal defect, and (4) buttress the medial tibia.
items.note: Directly tests classic, highly high-yield four-step surgical sequence.

items.q: A 48-year-old female presents after a fall with a lateral split-depression tibial plateau fracture. Which Schatzker type is this fracture, and what is its relative frequency among tibial plateau fractures?
o: Schatzker Type I; accounts for 10–15% of fractures
Schatzker Type III; accounts for 30–40% of fractures
Schatzker Type II; accounts for 55–70% of fractures
Schatzker Type IV; accounts for 50% of fractures
items.e: Schatzker Type II is a lateral split-depression fracture. It is the most common pattern of tibial plateau fracture, accounting for approximately 55% to 70% of cases.
items.note: Correct classification details and frequency figures matching reference notes.

items.q: During an anterolateral surgical approach to the distal tibia for open reduction and internal fixation of a pilon fracture, the interval between the extensor digitorum longus/peroneus tertius and the fibula is developed. Which nerve is directly at risk during this approach?
items.e: The anterolateral approach to the distal tibia/pilon is performed between the EDL/peroneus tertius and the fibula. The superficial peroneal nerve crosses this surgical field and is the primary nerve at risk.
items.note: Accurate anatomical structure at risk for standard surgical approach.

items.q: Intramedullary nailing of proximal-third tibial shaft fractures is technically challenging and prone to characteristic deformity. If blocking (Poller) screws or extended positioning techniques are not utilized, which typical malalignment of the proximal fragment occurs?
items.e: Proximal third tibial fractures typically deform into valgus and procurvatum (apex anterior) during intramedullary nailing due to muscular pull and nail insertion trajectory.
items.note: Classic exam question regarding intramedullary nailing of proximal tibia fractures.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding the fragment anatomy and ligamentous attachments in distal tibial pilon (plafond) fractures is CORRECT?
o: The posterolateral (Volkmann) fragment is attached to the calcaneofibular ligament
The anterolateral (Chaput) fragment remains attached to the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL)
The Chaput fragment represents central die-punch articular impaction
Associated fibular fractures occur in fewer than 25% of pilon cases
items.e: In tibial pilon fractures, the anterolateral Chaput fragment remains attached to the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL). Fibula fractures accompany pilon fractures in about 75% of cases.
items.note: Factually precise regarding pilon fracture anatomy.

items.q: During surgical elevation and rafting of a depressed articular fragment in a lateral tibial plateau fracture, subchondral void filler is placed to prevent re-collapse. Which of the following materials provides the greatest resistance to subchondral subsidence?
items.e: Calcium phosphate cement provides high initial compressive strength and resists subchondral articular subsidence best following elevation of depressed tibial plateau fragments.
items.note: Correct material property facts confirmed in Campbell's and notes.

items.q: Non-operative management using a Sarmiento functional brace is planned for a patient with a low-energy closed tibial shaft fracture. Which parameter represents the MAXIMUM acceptable deformity threshold for non-operative treatment?
o: Up to 10 degrees of varus/valgus angulation
Up to 20 degrees of AP angulation
Up to 15 degrees of rotational deformity
items.e: Criteria for acceptable non-operative alignment in tibial shaft fractures include <5 degrees varus/valgus, <10 degrees AP angulation, <1 cm shortening, and <10 degrees rotation.
items.note: Clear single-best-answer testing established Sarmiento non-operative alignment criteria.

items.q: According to the classic biomechanical study by Ramsey and Hamilton, a 1 mm lateral shift of the talus within the ankle mortise causes approximately what percentage reduction in the tibiotalar contact area?
items.e: Ramsey and Hamilton demonstrated that just 1 mm of lateral talar displacement reduces the tibiotalar contact area by approximately 42%, serving as the biomechanical rationale for achieving anatomical reduction of ankle fractures.
items.note: Accurate classic biomechanical value supported by Campbell's and standard reference notes.

items.q: A 28-year-old athlete sustains a foot injury following a fall with the foot in pronation subjected to an external rotation force. Radiographs show a medial malleolar fracture and disruption of the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament. According to the Lauge-Hansen classification system, which fibular injury pattern is expected as this injury mechanism progresses to stage III?
o: Transverse avulsion fracture of the fibula below the joint line
Short oblique fibular fracture at the level of the syndesmosis
High spiral fibular fracture located above the level of the syndesmosis
Comminuted fibular fracture at or above the syndesmosis with lateral comminution
items.e: A pronation-external rotation (PER) mechanism characteristically results in a high spiral fibular fracture above the syndesmosis (Weber C pattern) at stage III, following medial structure injury (stage I) and AITFL rupture (stage II).
items.note: Correct sequence and fracture pattern according to Lauge-Hansen PER mechanism.

items.q: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a twisting injury to his ankle. Ankle radiographs show significant widening of the medial clear space and syndesmotic space, but no distal fibular fracture is seen on the ankle series. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in clinical assessment?
o: Apply a walking boot and discharge with full weight-bearing
Palpate the entire fibula and obtain full-length tibiofibular radiographs to evaluate for a Maisonneuve fracture
Perform immediate open primary repair of the superficial deltoid ligament
Apply a non-weight-bearing cast for 12 weeks without further imaging
items.e: A Maisonneuve fracture consists of a proximal fibular fracture associated with disruption of the syndesmosis, interosseous membrane, and medial ankle structures. Palpating the entire fibula and taking full-length radiographs is essential whenever an apparently isolated medial ankle injury or syndesmotic widening is identified.
items.note: Standard emergency assessment protocol for suspected Maisonneuve fracture.

items.q: Which of the following radiographic parameters, measured on an AP ankle radiograph 1 cm above the tibial plafond, is considered the most reliable measure for diagnosing a syndesmotic injury?
o: Medial clear space greater than 2 mm
Tibiofibular clear space greater than 5–6 mm
items.e: A tibiofibular clear space greater than 5–6 mm on an AP radiograph (measured 1 cm proximal to the plafond) is recognized as the most reliable radiographic parameter for identifying a syndesmotic disruption.
items.note: Accurate radiographic definition standard in ankle trauma literature.

items.q: Based on evidence from randomized clinical trials (such as Kortekangas et al., BMJ 2019), isolated Weber B (supination-external rotation) lateral malleolar fractures confirmed to be stable on weight-bearing stress radiographs can be successfully managed non-operatively with immobilisation for what duration?
items.e: Kortekangas et al. (BMJ 2019) showed that stable (stress-negative) isolated Weber B fractures managed with 3 weeks of cast or orthosis immobilisation achieve functional outcomes and healing equivalent to those managed with traditional 6-week immobilisation.
items.note: High-yield evidence-based clinical trial landmark question.

items.q: During open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture, the operating surgeon applies lateral traction to the distal fibula using a bone hook to assess syndesmotic stability. What is the name of this intraoperative stability test?
items.e: The Cotton (hook) test is performed intraoperatively by pulling the fibula laterally with a bone hook; widening of more than approximately 2 mm indicates syndesmotic instability.
items.note: Standard surgical procedure test name.

items.q: During a standard lateral approach to the distal fibula for fracture fixation, which structure is at primary risk of injury when extending the skin incision proximally, as it pierces the deep crural fascia approximately 10 to 12 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus?
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve exits through the deep crural fascia about 10–12 cm proximal to the lateral malleolus tip and travels obliquely across the anterolateral aspect of the lower leg, placing it at risk during proximal extension of the lateral surgical approach to the fibula.
items.note: Anatomical landmark question frequently tested in orthopaedic surgical entrance exams.
items.reason: repeats fai20261123_067 (SPN in lateral fibular approach)

items.q: Radiographic criteria defined by Hertel are used to predict the risk of humeral head ischemia after proximal humerus fractures. Which of the following findings is considered one of these key predictors?
o: Metaphyseal extension under 8 mm attached to the posteromedial calcar
Disruption of the lateral periosteal hinge over 5 mm
Posterior displacement of the humeral shaft over 45 degrees
items.e: Hertel's predictors of humeral head ischemia include a metaphyseal calcar extension attached to the head of less than 8 mm, a disrupted medial hinge (displacement over 2 mm), and an anatomical neck fracture pattern.
items.note: Accurate, standard super-speciality exam question on Hertel's ischemia predictors.

items.q: A 65-year-old active female undergoes proximal humeral locking plate fixation for a displaced 3-part proximal humerus fracture. Two weeks postoperatively, radiograph shows loss of reduction into varus. Which surgical technical step is most critical to prevent this complication?
o: Placing the superior border of the plate 15 mm below the top of the greater tuberosity
Restoring medial calcar support with an inferomedial calcar screw
Routinely transposing the cephalic vein laterally into the deltoid muscle
Fixing the lesser tuberosity with a single 3.5 mm cortical screw
items.e: Restoration of medial calcar support (using an inferomedial calcar screw or fibular strut graft) is crucial to prevent secondary varus collapse and screw cut-out, which is the most common complication following locking plate fixation.
items.note: High-yield technical question regarding proximal humeral locking plates supported by standard literature.

items.q: A 52-year-old man sustains an acute traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation that is successfully reduced in the emergency department. Post-reduction radiographs confirm joint congruence without fracture. Physical examination reveals persistent weakness in active shoulder abduction and external rotation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Immediate surgical exploration for axillary nerve transection
Rigid immobilization in a sling for 8 weeks without imaging
Urgent MRI or ultrasound to evaluate for a rotator cuff tear
items.e: In patients over 40 years of age with anterior shoulder dislocation, rotator cuff tears are common. Persistent weakness after reduction requires prompt evaluation with MRI or ultrasound to assess cuff integrity.
items.note: Classic management question for older patients with shoulder dislocation.

items.q: A 28-year-old athlete sustains a clavicle fracture. Radiographs show a lateral-third clavicle fracture located medial to the coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments, with the medial fragment elevated and detached from the CC ligaments. According to Neer's classification, what is the fracture type and its primary clinical implication?
o: Type I; stable injury best treated non-operatively in a sling
Type III; intra-articular AC joint extension causing acute joint instability
Type IV; periosteal sleeve injury typically seen in young children
Type II; high non-union rate (about 30%) requiring surgical fixation
items.e: Neer Type II lateral clavicle fractures occur medial to the CC ligaments, resulting in detachment of the medial fragment from the ligaments. This leads to instability and a high non-union rate (~30%), warranting operative fixation.
items.note: Standard classification question with accurate clinical correlation.

items.q: A 30-year-old rugby player presents with shoulder pain after a direct blow. An axillary radiograph reveals that the distal clavicle is displaced posteriorly through the trapezius muscle. According to the Rockwood classification, how is this injury classified?
items.e: Rockwood Type IV acromioclavicular joint injury is characterized by posterior displacement of the clavicle into or through the trapezius fascia, best identified on an axillary view, and requires surgical treatment.
items.note: Clear and standard Rockwood classification question.

items.q: A 45-year-old man sustains a scapular fracture after a motor vehicle accident. CT reconstruction demonstrates an intra-articular glenoid fracture (Ideberg type). What articular step-off threshold is a standard indication for open reduction and internal fixation?
items.e: Displaced intra-articular glenoid fractures (Ideberg classification) are indicated for surgical fixation when there is an articular step-off exceeding 4–5 mm or a glenoid rim fracture causing persistent glenohumeral instability (>20–25% glenoid involvement).
items.note: Standard surgical indication threshold for glenoid fractures.

items.q: A 32-year-old male sustains a closed, mid-shaft transverse humeral fracture with an associated complete radial nerve palsy (wrist drop and sensory loss over the first dorsal web space). Radiographs show acceptable alignment (<20° anterior angulation, <30° varus, 1 cm shortening). What is the standard management for the radial nerve injury?
o: Non-operative treatment with a Sarmiento functional brace and clinical observation
Urgent surgical exploration of the radial nerve and open reduction internal fixation
Tendon transfer of pronator teres to ECRB within 2 weeks of presentation
Closed manipulation under anesthesia to free the entrapped nerve
items.e: Radial nerve palsy associated with a closed humeral shaft fracture is typically a neurapraxia (seen in ~12% of cases). The standard treatment is observation for 3–4 months; about 70–90% recover spontaneously. Exploration is reserved for open fractures or nerve failure to recover on EMG/clinical follow-up.
items.note: Classic exam question with standard evidence-based management.

items.q: Recent anatomical studies (e.g., Hettrich et al., 2010) have revised the classic understanding of humeral head vascularity. Which vessel is now recognized as providing the majority (approximately 64%) of the blood supply to the humeral head?
items.e: Although the anterior humeral circumflex artery and its arcuate artery (of Laing) were classically thought to be the primary supply, recent quantitative anatomical studies confirm that the posterior humeral circumflex artery supplies most of the humeral head (approximately 64%).
items.note: High-yield basic science/anatomy concept frequently tested in entrance exams.

items.q: A 38-year-old male presents with a posterior elbow dislocation associated with a comminuted radial head fracture and a coronoid process fracture ('terrible triad' injury). During surgical treatment via a lateral approach, what is the correct inside-out management sequence to restore stability?
o: MCL repair -> Coronoid fixation -> Radial head replacement -> LCL repair
Coronoid fixation -> Radial head fixation/replacement -> LCL repair -> MCL repair/ex-fix if unstable
Radial head excision -> LCL repair -> Coronoid fixation -> MCL repair
LCL repair -> Radial head replacement -> Coronoid fixation -> Hinged external fixator
items.e: The management sequence for terrible triad injuries of the elbow is: (1) coronoid fixation or anterior capsule repair, (2) radial head fixation or replacement (never excision), (3) LCL (LUCL) repair to the lateral epicondyle, and finally (4) MCL repair or a hinged external fixator if the elbow remains unstable.
items.note: Accurate sequence for surgical reconstruction of terrible triad injuries, fully aligned with standard orthopaedic guidelines.

items.q: A 74-year-old woman with osteoporotic bone sustains a low-energy, highly comminuted AO/OTA 13C3 distal humerus fracture. Total elbow arthroplasty (TEA) is chosen as the primary treatment based on the McKee trial. Which lifelong post-operative lifting restriction should the patient be counseled about?
o: Roughly 1 kg for repetitive lifting and about 5 kg for a single maximum lift
No single lift over 1 kg and complete prohibition of repetitive lifting
Up to 5 kg for repetitive lifting and 15 kg for a single maximum lift
No lifting restrictions are needed once the soft tissues are healed
items.e: Total elbow arthroplasty (linked semi-constrained) for unreconstructable C3 distal humerus fractures in elderly patients requires lifelong lifting restrictions of roughly 1 kg for repetitive activities and about 5 kg as a single max lift to avoid early mechanical failure.
items.note: Exact postoperative restrictions following total elbow arthroplasty as defined in Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics.

items.q: During surgical exposure of the radial head using the posterolateral Kocher approach (between the anconeus and extensor carpi ulnaris), which position of the forearm safest for preventing posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) injury?
o: 90 degrees of elbow flexion with neutral rotation
items.e: Pronating the forearm moves the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) anteriorly and medially away from the surgical field, reducing the risk of iatrogenic PIN nerve injury during posterolateral approaches (Kocher and Kaplan) to the radial head.
items.note: Standard surgical anatomy fact for elbow approaches.

items.q: A 28-year-old male undergoes open reduction and rigid plate fixation of a Galeazzi fracture. Intraoperatively, after restoring radial length and bow, the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) is tested in supination and found to be reducible but unstable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Perform an immediate distal ulna resection (Darrach procedure)
Immobilise the limb in full pronation in a long arm cast for 6 weeks
Apply a short arm cast in neutral rotation without additional stabilization
Pin the radius to the ulna with K-wires in supination
items.e: After rigid plate fixation of a Galeazzi fracture, the DRUJ must be evaluated. If the DRUJ is reducible but unstable in supination, the recommended management is to pin the radius to the ulna in supination (or repair the TFCC) and immobilise.
items.note: Standard management algorithm for Galeazzi fracture with persistent intraoperative DRUJ instability.

items.q: A 42-year-old male sustains an adult Monteggia fracture-dislocation characterized by a proximal ulnar shaft fracture with apex-posterior angulation, accompanied by posterior dislocation of the radial head and a radial head fracture. Which Bado classification type is this?
items.e: Bado Type II represents a posterior Monteggia injury (proximal ulnar fracture with apex-posterior angulation and posterior radial head dislocation), which is the commonest type seen in adults and is frequently accompanied by a radial head fracture.
items.note: Factually accurate classification question for Monteggia fractures.

items.q: To prevent 'overstuffing' during radial head arthroplasty—which leads to capitellar wear, lateral ulnohumeral joint gap, and loss of flexion—the proximal surface of the prosthetic head should be aligned with which anatomic landmark?
o: Flush with the apex of the olecranon process
Level with the proximal edge of the lesser sigmoid notch of the ulna
5 mm proximal to the tip of the coronoid process
Level with the distal border of the radial tuberosity
items.e: To avoid overstuffing the radiohumeral joint during radial head replacement, the top of the implant should sit precisely at the level of the proximal edge of the lesser sigmoid notch of the ulna (approximately 1 mm below the tip of the coronoid process).
items.note: Key anatomical reference landmark for radial head sizing and height restoration.

items.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a displaced, non-comminuted, transverse olecranon fracture. Radiographs show that the ulnohumeral joint is stable (Mayo Type IIA). What is the surgical procedure of choice?
o: Excision of the fragment with triceps advancement
Tension-band wiring using parallel K-wires and a figure-of-eight wire
Closed reduction and long-arm cast immobilization
items.e: Displaced, non-comminuted, transverse olecranon fractures with a stable ulnohumeral joint (Mayo IIA) are classically treated with tension-band wiring (TBW) using two parallel K-wires and a figure-of-eight wire to convert triceps tensile forces into articular compressive forces.
items.note: Classic management of Mayo Type IIA olecranon fractures.

items.q: A patient with a history of an elbow dislocation present with persistent symptomatic posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI). Deficiency of which structure is the primary cause, and which examination test best demonstrates this instability?
o: Lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL); Lateral pivot-shift test
Anterior bundle of the MCL; Valgus stress test
Transverse ligament of the MCL; Varus stress test
items.e: Posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) is caused by insufficiency of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL). The pathognomonic physical examination test is the lateral pivot-shift test of O'Driscoll (producing a reduction clunk around 40 degrees of flexion).
items.note: High-yield standard concept in elbow instability.

items.q: A 42-year-old female presents 5 weeks following cast immobilisation for an undisplaced distal radius fracture with a sudden inability to extend her thumb interphalangeal joint. What is the standard surgical treatment for this complication?
o: Extensor indicis proprius (EIP) to extensor pollicis longus (EPL) transfer
Flexor carpi radialis (FCR) to EPL transfer
items.e: EPL rupture after undisplaced distal radius fractures occurs 3 to 8 weeks later due to attrition at Lister's tubercle or ischaemia. The standard management is an extensor indicis proprius (EIP) to EPL tendon transfer.
items.note: Accurate, standard superspeciality-level question directly tested in entrance exams.

items.q: According to Lafontaine's criteria, which of the following features is NOT considered an indicator of distal radius fracture instability predicting loss of reduction in a cast?
items.e: Lafontaine's instability predictors include dorsal angulation >20°, dorsal comminution, intra-articular involvement, associated ulnar fracture, age >60 years, and initial shortening >5 mm. A radial inclination of 18° is within acceptable radiologic parameters (>15°) and is not a Lafontaine instability criterion.
items.note: Factually correct, unambiguous distractor based on standard criteria.

items.q: A 25-year-old male presents with an acute undisplaced (less than 1 mm displacement) fracture of the scaphoid waist. Based on the findings of the SWIFFT trial, what is the initial management of choice?
o: Immediate percutaneous screw fixation via a volar approach
Dorsal open reduction and internal fixation
Cast immobilisation, reserving surgical fixation for non-union
items.e: The SWIFFT trial (2020) demonstrated no long-term benefit of early surgical fixation over cast immobilisation for undisplaced or minimally displaced (<2 mm) scaphoid waist fractures. The recommended protocol is cast treatment, reserving surgery for non-union.
items.note: High-yield evidence-based question referencing modern standard trials.

items.q: Which stage of Mayfield's classification of perilunate instability represents a volar dislocation of the lunate, producing the classic 'spilled teacup' sign on a lateral radiograph?
items.e: Mayfield progression follows Stage I (scapholunate disruption), Stage II (lunocapitate disruption), Stage III (lunotriquetral disruption), and Stage IV (volar lunate dislocation with the 'spilled teacup' sign on lateral radiographs).
items.note: Standard classification question, clear single best answer.

items.q: A patient with Kienböck disease exhibits lunate collapse with fixed scaphoid rotation, a radioscaphoid angle greater than 60 degrees, and a cortical ring sign, but no pancarpal arthritis. Which Lichtman stage is present and what is the indicated management?
o: Stage IIIB; Proximal row carpectomy or STT/SC fusion
items.e: Lichtman Stage IIIB represents lunate collapse with fixed scaphoid rotation (scaphoid ring sign, radioscaphoid angle >60°). Surgical options for Stage IIIB include proximal row carpectomy (PRC) or STT/SC fusion, whereas joint-levelling radial shortening osteotomy is indicated for ulnar-negative stage I-IIIA.
items.note: Accurately tests staging and stage-specific operative decision-making.

items.q: According to the Palmer classification of triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) lesions, a traumatic peripheral ulnar detachment of the TFCC is classified as which pattern, and what is its definitive management?
items.e: Palmer Class 1 traumatic TFCC lesions include Class 1A (central perforation, treated with arthroscopic debridement) and Class 1B (peripheral ulnar detachment with or without ulnar styloid fracture, treated with surgical repair).
items.note: Standard classification and treatment pairing question.

items.q: In progressive osteoarthritic changes secondary to scaphoid non-union advanced collapse (SNAC wrist), which radiocarpal joint region is characteristically SPARED?
items.e: In a SNAC wrist, post-traumatic degenerative arthritis progresses sequentially from the radial styloid-scaphoid joint to the capitate-scaphoid and lunocapitate joints, characteristically sparing the radiolunate joint.
items.note: Classic high-yield anatomical/pathological exam concept.

items.q: During volar locking plate fixation of a distal radius fracture via the modified Henry approach, placing the plate distal to the watershed line increases the risk of rupture of which tendon?
items.e: Volar locking plates placed distal to the watershed line create plate prominence on the distal radius, leading to mechanical attrition and rupture of the flexor pollicis longus (FPL) tendon.
items.note: Surgically relevant, highly tested complication question.

items.q: A 28-year-old male undergoes reamed intramedullary nailing of a closed tibial shaft fracture. Six hours postoperatively, he complains of severe, unremitting leg pain exacerbated by passive extension of the toes. His diastolic blood pressure is 65 mmHg. Intra-compartmental pressure measurement of the anterior compartment demonstrates a pressure of 40 mmHg. What is the calculated delta pressure and the definitive next step in management?
o: Delta pressure is 25 mmHg; perform urgent four-compartment fasciotomy
Delta pressure is 25 mmHg; elevate the leg above heart level and observe for 2 hours
Delta pressure is 105 mmHg; reassure the patient and increase parenteral analgesia
Delta pressure is 40 mmHg; perform emergency CT angiography to evaluate arterial patency
items.e: Delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) is 65 - 40 = 25 mmHg. A delta pressure of less than 30 mmHg confirms compartment syndrome (McQueen criteria) and requires immediate four-compartment fasciotomy. Elevating the limb reduces arterial perfusion pressure and worsens tissue ischaemia.
items.note: The question accurately tests the McQueen criteria for compartment syndrome and the correct management sequence.

items.q: Which of the following statements correctly summarizes the key findings of the FLOW (Fluid Lavage of Open Wounds) trial regarding initial irrigation of open fractures?
o: Soap solution resulted in significantly lower infection rates than normal saline
High-pressure pulsatile lavage was superior to low-pressure lavage in reducing reoperation rates
Low-pressure irrigation with normal saline is as effective as high-pressure irrigation, and soap solution was associated with higher reoperation rates than saline
Additives such as bacitracin or chlorhexidine in high-pressure irrigation provide superior outcomes to plain saline
items.e: The landmark FLOW trial demonstrated that low-pressure irrigation with normal saline is equal in efficacy to high-pressure irrigation (and less costly), while soap solution was actually worse than saline, resulting in higher reoperation rates.
items.note: This is a landmark trial in orthopaedic trauma and is correctly represented.

items.q: According to the Early Appropriate Care (EAC) protocol described by Vallier et al., definitive internal fixation of long-bone fractures can be safely performed once resuscitation achieves which set of laboratory endpoints?
o: Serum lactate < 2.0 mmol/L, pH ≥ 7.40, and base excess ≥ 0 mmol/L
Serum lactate < 4.0 mmol/L, pH ≥ 7.25, and base excess ≥ -5.5 mmol/L
Serum lactate < 6.0 mmol/L, pH ≥ 7.15, and base excess ≥ -8.0 mmol/L
Serum lactate < 1.0 mmol/L, pH ≥ 7.35, and base excess ≥ -2.0 mmol/L
items.e: The Early Appropriate Care (EAC) protocol by Vallier establishes that definitive fracture fixation can proceed safely within 36 hours once resuscitation endpoints are met: serum lactate < 4.0 mmol/L, pH ≥ 7.25, and base excess ≥ -5.5 mmol/L.
items.note: The laboratory values match the established EAC criteria in the reference notes.

items.q: Which statement regarding limb salvage versus primary amputation in severe lower extremity trauma is accurate based on findings from the LEAP (Lower Extremity Assessment Project) study?
o: Initial absence of plantar sensation is an absolute indication for primary amputation
Primary amputation leads to significantly superior long-term functional scores compared to successful limb salvage at 2 and 7 years
A Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS) of 7 or more has near 100% predictive accuracy for amputation and should be used as the sole decision criterion
Approximately half of initially insensate feet regain plantar sensation by 2 years, and salvage yields functional outcomes similar to amputation at 2 and 7 years
items.e: The LEAP study established that an initially insensate foot is not an indication for amputation, as about half of insensate feet regain plantar sensation by 2 years. Furthermore, functional outcomes (Sickness Impact Profile) between limb salvage and primary amputation were similar at 2 and 7 years.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the major paradigm shifts introduced by the LEAP study.

items.q: During emergency decompression of the leg using a standard two-incision four-compartment fasciotomy, which neurovascular structures are at highest risk of injury along the posteromedial incision line?
o: Deep peroneal nerve and anterior tibial artery
Saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein
Sural nerve and short saphenous vein
items.e: The posteromedial incision for leg fasciotomy is placed about 2 cm posterior to the medial border of the tibia to release the superficial and deep posterior compartments. The saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein run near this line and must be identified and protected.
items.note: This tests surgical anatomy relevant to a common orthopaedic emergency.

items.q: A 35-year-old polytrauma patient following a high-speed motor vehicle collision has an estimated blood loss of 35% (approx. 1750 mL). On arrival, his heart rate is 132 bpm, blood pressure shows a drop in systolic pressure, mental state is confused, and base deficit is -7 mmol/L. According to ATLS classification, this patient is in which class of haemorrhagic shock?
items.e: Class III haemorrhagic shock (ATLS) is characterized by 30-40% blood loss, heart rate 120-140 bpm, decreased systolic blood pressure, confused mental state, and base deficit between -6 and -10 mmol/L.
items.note: The clinical parameters provided perfectly match the ATLS Class III shock definition.

items.q: Which of the following standards is recommended by current orthoplastic guidelines (BOAST 4 / BAPRAS-BOA) and trials for managing severe open fractures?
o: Negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) significantly reduces deep infection rates compared to standard dressings prior to definitive cover
Definitive soft-tissue coverage ('fix and flap') should ideally be achieved within 72 hours of injury
Systemic prophylactic antibiotics should be continued for at least 14 days post-operatively
Initial debridement should be delayed beyond 48 hours to allow clear tissue demarcation
items.e: Current BOAST/BAPRAS standards recommend definitive soft-tissue cover within 72 hours ('fix and flap'). The WOLLF trial showed no difference in infection rates between NPWT and standard dressings, placing NPWT strictly as a temporary dressing.
items.note: The question tests current evidence-based guidelines and the results of the WOLLF trial.

items.q: A 24-year-old male sustains a high-energy knee dislocation resulting in complete disruption of the popliteal artery. The warm ischaemia time is 4 hours. What is the correct sequence of surgical steps for optimal limb salvage?
o: Temporary vascular shunt → skeletal stabilization → definitive vascular repair → prophylactic fasciotomy
Skeletal stabilization → temporary vascular shunt → definitive vascular repair → prophylactic fasciotomy
Definitive vascular repair → skeletal stabilization → prophylactic fasciotomy
Prophylactic fasciotomy → definitive vascular repair → skeletal stabilization
items.e: When arterial injury threatens a limb, inserting a temporary vascular shunt first restores distal arterial flow within the 6-hour golden window. Skeletal fixation (e.g. external fixator) is performed next to protect the vascular repair, followed by definitive vascular repair and prophylactic compartment fasciotomy.
items.note: This is the standard damage-control sequence for combined vascular and orthopaedic injuries.

items.q: A 35-year-old male presents with persistent pain and an audible 'click' at the fracture site 8 months after static intramedullary nailing of a transverse femoral shaft fracture. Radiographs show exuberant 'elephant foot' callus at the fracture ends that fails to bridge the gap. What is the most appropriate management according to the Weber-Cech classification of non-union?
o: Debridement, resection of callus, and autologous bone grafting
Exchange reamed intramedullary nailing with a larger diameter nail
Open reduction and internal fixation with a locking compression plate and BMP-7
items.e: This is a hypertrophic non-union, which indicates good biology but inadequate stability. Treatment focuses on improving stability (e.g., exchange reamed nailing to increase fit and stability) rather than adding biology like bone grafts.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the management of a hypertrophic non-union based on the Weber-Cech classification and standard orthopaedic practice for femoral shaft non-unions.

items.q: According to Perren’s Strain Theory, what is the maximum percentage of interfragmentary strain that allows for primary (direct) bone healing to occur?
items.e: Primary bone healing requires absolute stability with an interfragmentary strain of less than 2%. Strain between 2-10% leads to secondary bone healing (callus formation), while strain over 10% results in fibrous tissue or non-union.
items.note: This is a fundamental concept in fracture biomechanics and is accurately represented according to the provided notes and Perren's theory.

items.q: During the histological stages of secondary bone healing, which type of collagen is specifically associated with hypertrophic chondrocytes during the calcification phase of the soft callus?
items.e: While Type II collagen is predominant in the cartilaginous soft callus and Type I in the hard callus (woven bone), Type X collagen is specifically produced by hypertrophic chondrocytes as the cartilage matrix prepares for calcification and endochondral ossification.
items.note: The question tests specific histological knowledge of bone healing stages as detailed in the reference notes.

items.q: Which of the following modifications to a unilateral external fixator construct provides the most significant increase in the mechanical stiffness of the frame?
o: Increasing the distance between the connecting bar and the bone
Placing the pins as far from the fracture site as possible
Increasing the diameter of the Schanz pins
Using a carbon fiber bar instead of a stainless steel bar
items.e: Pin diameter is the most important factor for stiffness because the bending stiffness of a pin is proportional to the fourth power of its radius. Other ways to increase stiffness include placing pins closer to the fracture and the bar closer to the bone.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the most influential variable in external fixator biomechanics.

items.q: A surgeon is performing an open reduction and internal fixation for a simple transverse fracture of the olecranon. To utilize the tension band principle effectively, the wire construct should be placed on which surface to convert tensile forces into compressive forces?
items.e: The tension band principle requires the implant to be placed on the tension (convex) side of the bone. In the olecranon, the posterior surface is the tension side; the wire converts the pull of the triceps into compression across the articular surface.
items.note: This is a classic application of the tension band principle as described in AO principles and the reference notes.

items.q: Based on the results of the BESTT trial, recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) is FDA approved for use in which of the following clinical scenarios?
o: Acute open tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nailing
Posterolateral fusion in the cervical spine
Critical-sized segmental defects of the radius
items.e: The BESTT trial provided the evidence for FDA approval of rhBMP-2 specifically for acute open tibial fractures treated with intramedullary nailing, demonstrating a reduced rate of secondary interventions.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the specific trial and FDA approval mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: In the Masquelet (induced membrane) technique for managing a 7 cm segmental bone defect, what is the primary purpose of the second stage of the procedure?
o: To debride the necrotic bone and place a PMMA cement spacer
To remove the spacer and fill the biological membrane with cancellous autograft
To perform a vascularized fibular transfer into the induced membrane
To perform a corticotomy for distraction osteogenesis
items.e: The Masquelet technique is a two-stage procedure. Stage 1 involves debridement and placing a cement spacer to induce a vascular membrane. Stage 2 (usually at 4-8 weeks) involves removing the spacer and filling the membrane with bone graft.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the steps of the Masquelet technique as described in the reference notes.

items.q: When performing distraction osteogenesis using the Ilizarov technique, what is the standard rate and rhythm of distraction used to ensure high-quality regenerate formation in an adult patient?
items.e: The standard distraction protocol for Ilizarov bone transport is 1 mm per day, delivered in four increments of 0.25 mm (rhythm) after an initial latency period of 5-7 days.
items.note: The question accurately tests the standard rate and rhythm of distraction osteogenesis as per Ilizarov principles.

items.q: A 32-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle accident. He is alert and oriented (GCS 15) but reports neck pain. He has no focal neurological deficits, no distracting injuries, and no signs of intoxication. On examination, there is tenderness over the posterior midline of the cervical spine. According to the NEXUS criteria, what is the next step in management?
o: Range-of-motion assessment; if he can rotate 45 degrees, no imaging is needed
CT scan of the cervical spine as the first-line imaging
MRI to evaluate for disco-ligamentous injury
items.e: Under NEXUS criteria, the presence of midline cervical tenderness necessitates imaging. CT is the first-line imaging modality in adult trauma as it is more sensitive than radiographs for detecting fractures at the craniocervical and cervicothoracic junctions.
items.note: Correctly applies NEXUS criteria and identifies CT as the gold standard first-line imaging in adult trauma.

items.q: A patient with a Jefferson burst fracture of the atlas undergoes an open-mouth odontoid radiograph, which reveals a combined lateral mass overhang of 8.5 mm. An MRI confirms a midsubstance rupture of the transverse atlantal ligament (TAL). According to the Rule of Spence and the Dickman classification, what is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Halo-vest immobilization to allow bony healing
items.e: A combined overhang of >6.9 mm (or 8.1 mm with magnification) suggests TAL rupture (Rule of Spence). Dickman Type I (midsubstance) injuries of the TAL do not heal with immobilization and require C1-C2 fusion, whereas Type II (bony avulsion) may heal in a collar or halo.
items.note: Accurately combines the Rule of Spence threshold with the Dickman classification for TAL injuries.

items.q: A 45-year-old female presents with a Type II odontoid fracture. CT imaging demonstrates that the fracture line runs obliquely from the anteroinferior aspect of the dens to the posterosuperior aspect of the C2 body. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical intervention for this specific fracture pattern?
o: Primary C1-C2 transarticular screw fixation (Magerl technique)
items.e: This is a Grauer Type IIC fracture (oblique from anteroinferior to posterosuperior). Unlike Type IIB (anterosuperior to posteroinferior), an anterior screw in a Type IIC fracture would be parallel to the fracture line and cause shearing; therefore, posterior C1-C2 fusion is indicated.
items.note: Tests the specific contraindication for anterior odontoid screws based on fracture obliquity (Grauer classification).

items.q: A 24-year-old male sustains a traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (Hangman's fracture) after a diving accident. Radiographs show significant angulation of C2 on C3 with minimal translation (2 mm). The fracture line is noted to be oblique. Which of the following management steps is strictly contraindicated in this patient?
o: Application of a rigid cervical collar
items.e: This patient has a Levine-Edwards Type IIA Hangman's fracture, characterized by severe angulation and minimal translation (flexion-distraction mechanism). Traction is contraindicated in Type IIA as it can significantly worsen the distraction and angulation; reduction is achieved with compression and extension.
items.note: Tests a critical 'never-event' in spine trauma management (traction in Type IIA Hangman's).

items.q: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with a bilateral facet dislocation at C5-C6 following a fall. The patient is currently obtunded and cannot cooperate with a neurological examination. What is the mandatory next step before proceeding with reduction of the dislocation?
o: Immediate closed reduction with Gardner-Wells tongs
items.e: In an obtunded or uncooperative patient, an MRI must be performed before reduction to exclude a herniated disc. If a disc is present behind the vertebral body, closed reduction could potentially push the disc material into the cord, causing neurological deterioration.
items.note: Tests the standard protocol for facet reduction in the obtunded patient versus the awake patient.

items.q: An elderly patient with known cervical spondylosis presents with weakness in his hands and forearms after a hyperextension injury. Lower extremity power is 4/5, while intrinsic hand muscle power is 2/5. He has preserved perianal sensation and voluntary anal contraction. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?
o: It is the rarest of the incomplete spinal cord syndromes
It has the worst prognosis for recovery among incomplete syndromes
Walking and bowel/bladder function usually recover well
It is caused by injury to the dorsal columns
items.e: Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete SCI, typically caused by hyperextension in an elderly spondylotic spine. It features upper limb weakness (especially hands) worse than lower limbs. It has a good prognosis; walking and bowel/bladder function usually recover, though hand function is the least likely to fully recover.
items.note: Tests the most common incomplete cord syndrome, its classic presentation, and prognosis.

items.q: A 65-year-old male with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis presents to the emergency room with new-onset neck pain after a minor bump to the head. Initial cervical radiographs appear normal. What is the most appropriate course of action?
o: Reassurance and discharge with a soft collar
Flexion-extension radiographs to assess for dynamic instability
CT and MRI of the entire spine
Repeat radiographs in 2 weeks to look for a callus
items.e: In patients with ankylosing spondylitis or DISH, minor trauma can cause highly unstable 'chalk-stick' fractures. These are frequently missed on radiographs and can lead to late neurological deterioration or epidural hematomas. Whole-spine CT or MRI is mandatory regardless of initial radiographic findings.
items.note: Highlights the high index of suspicion required for fractures in the ankylosed spine.

items.q: A patient with a complete C6 spinal cord injury (ASIA A) is being evaluated for long-term rehabilitation goals. Which of the following functional milestones is most characteristic of this level of injury?
o: Requirement for a ventilator due to phrenic nerve palsy
Ability to achieve elbow extension and independent transfers
Use of a tenodesis grip for grasping objects
Full hand function including little finger abduction
items.e: C6 is the level of wrist extension, which allows for a tenodesis grip (passive finger flexion when the wrist is extended). Patients with C6 injuries can often achieve independent transfers and manual wheelchair use with adaptations. Elbow extension (triceps) is a C7 function.
items.note: Tests functional levels of SCI, specifically the hallmark tenodesis grip of C6.

items.q: A 32-year-old man presents with an L1 burst fracture after a fall. Neurological examination reveals grade 3/5 power in the lower limbs and preserved perianal sensation (incomplete cord injury). MRI shows no STIR hyperintensity in the interspinous ligaments or ligamentum flavum. What is the TLICS (Thoracolumbar Injury Classification and Severity) score for this patient?
items.e: The TLICS score is calculated as: Morphology = 2 (Burst); Neurology = 3 (Incomplete cord injury); PLC = 0 (Intact). Total = 5. A score of 5 or more indicates that operative management is recommended.
items.note: The calculation accurately reflects the TLICS components for a burst fracture with incomplete neurological deficit and intact posterior ligamentous complex.

items.q: According to the 2013 AO Spine Thoracolumbar Classification, a flexion-distraction injury characterized by a transosseous failure of the posterior tension band (bony Chance fracture) is classified as:
items.e: In the AO Spine classification, Type B1 is a transosseous posterior tension band disruption (bony Chance), B2 is a ligamentous tension band disruption, and B3 is a hyperextension injury (anterior tension band disruption).
items.note: The classification matches the 2013 AO Spine system where B1 is specifically the bony tension band failure.

items.q: A 24-year-old male sustains an L2 burst fracture (AO Type A3) after a fall from a height. He is neurologically intact (ASIA E). CT shows 45% canal compromise and 15 degrees of local kyphosis. MRI confirms the posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) is intact. Based on the randomized controlled trial evidence by Wood et al., what is the most appropriate management?
items.e: For neurologically intact burst fractures with an intact PLC (TLICS 2-3), Wood et al. demonstrated that non-operative treatment (with or without a brace) yields functional outcomes similar to surgery at long-term follow-up.
items.note: The question tests a landmark RCT mentioned in the reference notes regarding the management of stable burst fractures.

items.q: A patient is brought to the emergency department following a motor vehicle accident where he was restrained by a lap belt only. Imaging reveals a flexion-distraction injury at L1. Which of the following associated findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
items.e: Flexion-distraction (Chance) injuries are associated with intra-abdominal visceral injuries, such as bowel perforation or mesenteric tears, in 40-50% of cases (the 'seat-belt sign').
items.note: The association between Chance fractures and abdominal visceral injury is a classic exam fact supported by the notes.

items.q: A 70-year-old man with Ankylosing Spondylitis falls and sustains a T12 hyperextension injury. Which of the following is a critical consideration in the management of this patient?
o: These fractures are usually stable and can be treated with a soft collar
The spine should be immobilized in a neutral or slightly extended position
Surgical fixation should ideally involve at least 3 levels above and below the fracture
Steroids should be administered routinely to prevent epidural haematoma
items.e: Fractures in ankylosed spines are highly unstable due to the long lever arms of the fused segments. Management requires long-segment posterior fixation (at least 2-3 levels above and below) and immobilization in the patient's pre-injury kyphotic position.
items.note: The management of fractures in ankylosing spondylitis requires long-segment fixation and specific positioning, as noted in the reference.

items.q: In the surgical management of a thoracolumbar burst fracture, the success of indirect decompression of retropulsed fragments via ligamentotaxis primarily depends on the integrity of the:
items.e: Ligamentotaxis uses the tension of the longitudinal ligaments to pull retropulsed bone fragments back into the vertebral body. This technique specifically requires an intact Posterior Longitudinal Ligament (PLL).
items.note: The role of the PLL in ligamentotaxis is a fundamental biomechanical principle in spine trauma surgery.

items.q: A 14-year-old athlete presents with acute back pain and radiculopathy after a heavy lifting session. Lateral radiographs show a small bony fragment at the posterior-superior margin of the L4 vertebral body. This injury is most likely a:
items.e: Apophyseal ring fractures (slipped vertebral apophysis) occur in adolescents. The fragment is displaced into the canal, often behaving clinically like a disc herniation and sometimes requiring surgical excision.
items.note: The clinical presentation and radiographic description are characteristic of a pediatric apophyseal ring fracture.

items.q: The 'watershed zone' of the spinal cord, characterized by a tenuous blood supply making it highly susceptible to ischemic injury during trauma, is located at which levels?
items.e: The thoracic spinal canal is narrowest and the blood supply is most tenuous between T4 and T9, which is considered the watershed zone of the spinal cord.
items.note: The T4-T9 watershed zone is a standard anatomical fact in spinal cord injury literature.

items.q: When tapping the brachioradialis tendon of a patient with suspected cervical myelopathy, the clinician observes finger flexion but a diminished contraction of the brachioradialis muscle. This 'inverted radial reflex' typically localizes the pathology to which level?
items.e: The inverted brachioradialis (radial) reflex is an upper motor neurone sign where tapping the brachioradialis produces finger flexion and reduced brachioradialis contraction, indicating a lesion at the C5-C6 level.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the clinical localization of the inverted radial reflex as described in the reference notes.

items.q: A 62-year-old male presents with worsening gait imbalance and clumsy hands. His modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score is calculated as 13. According to the AO Spine/WFNS guidelines, what is the most appropriate management?
o: Observation with repeat MRI in 12 months
items.e: An mJOA score of 12-14 is classified as moderate degenerative cervical myelopathy. For moderate and severe DCM (mJOA < 15), surgery is recommended to halt progression and improve function.
items.note: The question correctly applies the mJOA severity classification and the corresponding AO Spine/WFNS management guidelines.

items.q: Which MRI finding in a patient with degenerative cervical myelopathy is most strongly associated with irreversible cord cavitation (myelomalacia) and a poorer prognosis for functional recovery?
o: Obliteration of the anterior CSF space
items.e: While T2 hyperintensity alone can represent reversible oedema, the presence of T1 hypointensity along with T2 hyperintensity indicates myelomalacia/cavitation, which is irreversible and predicts a worse prognosis.
items.note: The distinction between T1 and T2 signal changes regarding prognosis is a high-yield exam fact supported by the notes.

items.q: A patient has multilevel ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL). The lateral radiograph shows that the OPLL mass crosses the K-line (the line connecting the midpoints of the spinal canal at C2 and C7). This 'K-line negative' status suggests:
o: Posterior decompression is likely to fail
Laminoplasty is the procedure of choice
items.e: A K-line negative status (where the OPLL crosses the line connecting the midpoints of the canal at C2 and C7) and an occupying ratio over 60% predict the failure of posterior decompression; an anterior approach or posterior fusion is preferred.
items.note: The definition and clinical implication of K-line status in OPLL management are correctly stated.

items.q: A 58-year-old female with 4-level cervical spondylotic myelopathy is being considered for a Hirabayashi open-door laminoplasty. Which of the following findings would be an absolute contraindication for this specific procedure?
items.e: Laminoplasty requires preserved lordosis so the spinal cord can drift dorsally away from anterior compressive structures. It is contraindicated in kyphosis because the cord cannot drift back.
items.note: The requirement for lordosis in posterior motion-preserving surgery is a fundamental principle of cervical spine surgery.

items.q: Following an anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF), a patient reports difficulty swallowing. According to clinical statistics, which is the most common postoperative complication of anterior cervical surgery?
items.e: Dysphagia is the most common complication after anterior cervical surgery. It is usually transient but occurs more frequently with multilevel procedures.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the most common complication as per standard orthopaedic literature and the provided notes.

items.q: During a physical examination, a patient is asked to keep their fingers extended and adducted. The clinician notices the little and ring fingers spontaneously drift into abduction and flexion within 30 seconds. This 'finger escape sign' is a feature of:
o: Ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow
items.e: The finger escape sign (Ono's sign) is a clinical feature of cervical myelopathy where the ulnar intrinsic weakness causes the little and ring fingers to drift into abduction and flexion when held in extension/adduction.
items.note: The eponym and clinical description are accurate and relevant for a superspeciality exam.

items.q: Which of the following clinical findings would most strongly suggest a diagnosis of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) rather than Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy (DCM)?
items.e: ALS is a key differential for DCM. ALS is characterized by the absence of sensory signs and the presence of fasciculations (including the tongue) and specific EMG findings. DCM typically includes sensory symptoms like numb hands.
items.note: The differential diagnosis between ALS and DCM is a common exam theme, and the distinguishing features used here are correct.

items.q: Regarding the composition and nutrition of the adult intervertebral disc, which of the following statements is correct based on its physiological characteristics?
o: The nucleus pulposus is primarily composed of Type I collagen
It is the largest avascular structure in the body, nourished by diffusion through endplates
Degeneration is characterized by an increase in the water to proteoglycan ratio
The annulus fibrosus consists of randomly oriented collagen fibers
items.e: The intervertebral disc is the largest avascular structure in the body and receives its nutrition via diffusion through the vertebral endplates. Degeneration involves a loss of water and proteoglycans and an increase in the Type I to Type II collagen ratio.
items.note: The question is factually correct and matches the provided reference notes regarding disc anatomy and nutrition.

items.q: A 48-year-old patient with chronic low back pain undergoes an MRI which demonstrates Modic Type I changes at the L5-S1 endplates. What are the characteristic signal findings on T1 and T2 weighted sequences for this stage?
items.e: Modic Type I changes represent inflammatory edema and are characterized by low signal on T1 and high signal on T2 weighted images. This stage is most strongly associated with active low back pain.
items.note: The MRI signal characteristics for Modic changes are accurately represented and follow standard orthopaedic teaching.

items.q: A 52-year-old male presents with weakness in the quadriceps and a diminished knee jerk reflex. MRI reveals a far lateral (extraforaminal) disc herniation at the L4-L5 level. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
items.e: In the lumbar spine, a far lateral (foraminal/extraforaminal) disc herniation compresses the exiting nerve root at that level (e.g., L4 at L4-L5). A standard paracentral herniation at L4-L5 would compress the traversing L5 root.
items.note: The anatomical relationship between disc herniation location and the affected nerve root is a classic exam topic and is correctly stated.

items.q: In the management of Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES), which clinical scenario is classified as 'Incomplete' (CES-I) and is generally associated with a better prognosis if operated upon promptly?
o: Bilateral sciatica with normal bladder function (Suspected CES)
Painless urinary retention with overflow incontinence
Altered urinary sensation or poor stream but without established retention
Total loss of bowel and bladder control with saddle anesthesia
items.e: CES-I (Incomplete) is defined by urinary difficulties such as altered sensation, poor stream, or needing to strain, but without established retention. CES-R (Retention) carries a worse prognosis. Surgery is ideally performed before retention develops.

items.q: A 72-year-old female presents with bilateral leg pain and heaviness that worsens with walking and standing upright. She finds significant relief when leaning forward on a shopping cart or sitting down. Which of the following findings would most likely distinguish this as neurogenic rather than vascular claudication?

Symptoms are worse when cycling than when walking
Pulses are absent in the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries
Symptoms are relieved by sitting or spinal flexion
items.e: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by spinal flexion (sitting or leaning forward) because it increases the canal area. Vascular claudication is typically relieved by simply stopping the activity (standing still) and is often associated with absent pulses and pain during cycling.

items.q: During a school screening programme using a scoliometer, at what minimum threshold should a child with a rib hump be referred for a standing PA radiograph to assess for scoliosis?

items.q: A 5-year-old child is diagnosed with congenital scoliosis. Which of the following vertebral anomalies is associated with the worst prognosis for curve progression, often exceeding 5 degrees per year?

items.note: The question correctly applies the Sorensen criteria for Scheuermann disease as defined in the notes.

items.note: The question correctly identifies the risk group for the crankshaft phenomenon based on skeletal maturity markers.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman presents 3 weeks after an uneventful total knee arthroplasty with an acutely swollen, warm knee and wound erythema. In this early post-operative period (within 6 weeks of surgery), normal inflammatory markers are physiologically elevated. Which diagnostic threshold combination is specified by the 2018 ICM criteria to diagnose periprosthetic joint infection in this setting?
o: Synovial WBC > 3,000 cells/µL, PMN > 80%, serum CRP > 10 mg/L
Synovial WBC > 10,000 cells/µL, PMN > 90%, serum CRP > 100 mg/L
Synovial WBC > 25,000 cells/µL, PMN > 75%, serum CRP > 50 mg/L
Synovial WBC > 50,000 cells/µL, PMN > 95%, serum CRP > 150 mg/L

The lower thresholds (WBC > 3,000 cells/µL, PMN > 80%, CRP > 10 mg/L) apply to chronic periprosthetic infections.
items.note: Standard high-yield concept regarding altered diagnostic thresholds in the early post-operative window.

items.q: A 72-year-old female presents 18 days following primary total hip arthroplasty with persistent wound erythema, continuous serosanguinous discharge, and fever. According to the Tsukayama classification, this infection is classified as which type, and what is the reported success rate of debridement and implant retention for this group?
items.e: Under the Tsukayama classification, Type 1 represents early post-operative infection occurring within the first month of surgery. items.q: A patient undergoing revision total knee arthroplasty for unexplained pain has an inconclusive pre-operative 2018 ICM score of 4. During surgery, intraoperative tissue samples are obtained. According to the 2018 ICM criteria, which of the following intraoperative findings is assigned 3 points toward the cumulative diagnostic score?

Histology demonstrating > 5 neutrophils per high-power field in 5 or more fields
Severe fibrous membrane formation with extensive metallosis
Synovial fluid leukocyte esterase reading of 1+
items.e: In the 2018 ICM intraoperative criteria, positive histology (> 5 neutrophils per HPF in 5 or more high-power fields) and gross intraoperative purulence are each assigned 3 points. A single positive intraoperative culture yields 2 points. Adding 3 points to an inconclusive pre-operative score of 4 achieves 7 points, confirming infection.
items.note: Accurate, testing the specific point allocation of intraoperative criteria under the 2018 ICM consensus.

items.q: Regarding the pathogenesis and microbiology of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), which of the following statements is correct?
o: Sessile bacteria in mature biofilm are approximately 50 to 100 times more resistant to antibiotics than planktonic forms
Biofilm maturation on prosthetic biomaterial surfaces typically requires 3 to 4 months
Coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus combined account for only 25-30% of all PJI cases
Polymicrobial infections account for approximately 10-15% of all periprosthetic joint infections
items.e: Polymicrobial infections account for approximately 10-15% of all periprosthetic joint infections. Sessile bacteria within biofilm glycocalyx are up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics than planktonic forms, biofilm matures within about 3-4 weeks, and staphylococcal species (CoNS and S. aureus) account for 50-60% of all cases.
items.note: Directly supported by standard literature and consensus notes; distractors have clear factual errors.

items.q: A 62-year-old male is being medically evaluated prior to elective primary total knee arthroplasty.
